Matthew 5:17.excerpt: Early commentators read 'fulfil' not as discarding the Law but as bringing out its full and intended meaning, with Christ as its goal.

Matthew 5:17.text: In first-century Jewish usage, to 'fulfil' the Law contrasts with 'abolishing' it; the phrase frames continuity with the Hebrew Scriptures rather than rupture.
Paul echoes the same logic: faith does not abolish the law but upholds it.
The very next verse stresses the enduring authority of the Law 'till all be fulfilled.'

turn the other cheek.excerpt: Classic commentators understood the saying as refusing retaliation and the cycle of revenge, not as endorsing abuse or injustice.
turn the other cheek.source: Public-domain patristic commentary (New Advent, Fathers of the Church)

turn the other cheek.text: A backhanded blow to the right cheek was, in the first-century Mediterranean world, an act of insult and dishonor directed at a social inferior; the response reframes the dynamic of honor and shame.
Paul develops the same ethic: do not repay evil for evil, but overcome evil with good.
Jesus himself is held up as the model: when reviled, he did not revile in return.

judge not.excerpt: Chrysostom notes that Christ does not forbid every judgment, but the harsh, censorious judging of a neighbor's faults by one who overlooks his own greater failings.
judge not.source: Public-domain patristic commentary (New Advent, Fathers of the Church)

judge not.text: The 'measure for measure' image in the saying draws on a common rabbinic idiom in which the standard a person uses toward others becomes the standard applied back to them.
Jesus commands to 'judge righteous judgment,' showing that discernment itself is not condemned, only hypocritical condemnation.
Paul warns that the one who judges another condemns himself, because he practices the same things.

ask and it will be given.excerpt: Augustine observes that God delays or withholds not from unwillingness but to enlarge our desire, so that what we receive may be held with a fuller joy.

ask and it will be given.text: The three verbs ask, seek, and knock stand in the Greek present tense, a continuous aspect that pictures sustained, persevering prayer rather than a single petition.
Luke's parallel pairs the promise with the gift of the Holy Spirit as the good gift the Father delights to give.
James balances the promise: some ask and do not receive because they ask wrongly, to spend on their own pleasures.

narrow gate.excerpt: The classic commentators note that the gate is called narrow because it is entered through self-denial and obedience, yet it opens onto life, while the broad road, easy at first, ends in destruction.

narrow gate.text: The 'two ways' image, a path of life and a path of death, was a familiar moral motif in Second Temple Judaism and the early church, as seen in early Christian catechetical writing.
Jesus urges, 'Strive to enter in at the strait gate,' underscoring effort and earnestness.
Moses sets life and death before the people and bids them 'choose life,' the Old Testament root of the two-ways choice.

born again.excerpt: Augustine explains that the birth 'from above' is the work of the Spirit in baptism and faith, a wholly new beginning that flesh cannot accomplish of itself.
born again.locator: Tractates on the Gospel of John, Tractate 11-12

born again.text: The Greek word rendered 'again' (anothen) also means 'from above'; Nicodemus hears a second physical birth, while Jesus intends a birth originating from God, a deliberate double meaning in the dialogue.
Jesus restates the saying: one must be born 'of water and of the Spirit' to enter the kingdom of God.
Peter speaks of being 'born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God.'

i am the way the truth and the life.excerpt: Augustine writes that Christ is the way by which we go, and the truth and life to which we go: walking by him as the way, we come to him as our rest.
i am the way the truth and the life.locator: Tractates on the Gospel of John, Tractate 69

i am the way the truth and the life.text: The saying answers Thomas's question about the road to the Father; in its setting it is not a comparison of religions but a word of comfort to disciples facing Jesus' departure.
Jesus had already said, 'I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved,' a kindred image of access.
Hebrews speaks of a 'new and living way' opened for us to approach God, echoing the same access theme.
